analysis.investment_thesis: ACME Solar is a highly leveraged solar IPP (Debt/EBITDA ~7.9x) that listed via IPO in late 2024 — precisely when renewable energy enthusiasm peaked — with revenue that has actually contracted 4.6% per annum over 5 years, ROE of only 7.57% barely above a risk-free rate, and free cash flow of -INR 1,719 Cr in FY25. The equity is a thin sliver sitting atop a INR 11,000 Cr debt mountain.
key_strengths: Operating CF has been positive all 5 years (5/5), confirming existing projects do generate cash from contracted power purchase agreements
Massive 3,780 MW under-development pipeline could significantly grow EBITDA once commissioned, with long-term government-backed PPAs providing revenue visibility
Operating margin of 65.28% reflects the economics of mature solar assets — once debt is serviced, the cash flow per MW is attractive
key_risks: Total debt of INR 10,976 Cr vs EBITDA of INR 1,396 Cr = Debt/EBITDA of 7.9x — finance costs (INR 759 Cr) consume 54% of EBITDA, leaving almost nothing for equity holders after reinvestment
Revenue has contracted at -4.6% CAGR over 5 years; the growth story is all in future project commissioning, which carries execution, tariff, and grid curtailment risks
FCF of -INR 1,719 Cr in FY25 means the company requires continuous access to capital markets — any tightening of credit or equity sentiment directly threatens solvency trajectory
red_flags: IPO listed November 2024 — classic cycle-peak issuance when renewable sentiment was at maximum optimism; promoters raised capital at the top
Promoter holds 83.29% — low public float amplifies volatility and limits price discovery, and any promoter pledge unwinding creates asymmetric downside
ROE of 7.57% is barely above India's 10-year G-Sec yield; P/E of 36.8x means the market is paying a 36-year payback for a 7.5% equity return — deeply irrational
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Solar IPPs are infrastructure businesses masquerading as growth stocks when listed. The economic reality is: you build an asset, lever it 4-5x, earn a contracted return spread over the cost of debt, and slowly delever over 20-25 years. At 36.8x P/E for 7.57% ROE, the market is pricing ACMESOLAR as if it were a technology compounder, not a utility with a 20-year payback horizon burdened by INR 11,000 Cr of debt.

The FY25 investing outflow of -INR 3,976 Cr tells you this company is in hyper-expansion mode, funded almost entirely by debt (financing CF +INR 3,408 Cr). If the next 3,780 MW of capacity is commissioned on time, at the right tariffs, with no curtailment, the forward story improves — but that's a chain of optimistic assumptions. My philosophy demands I ask: what is the floor? With D/E of 2.72x and negative FCF, the floor for equity is uncomfortably close to zero in a stress scenario. The IPO timing alone would make me deeply cautious. I require a far larger margin of safety before touching this name.
